categories.label: Fragmentation and Interest Misalignment in Off-site Supply Chains
categories.memo: Covers the structural fragmentation between factory/manufacturer and site-based parties, the divergent interests of independent for-profit organisations, and how this misalignment undermines natural coordination absent contractual mechanisms.

codes.label: Fragmented, multi-tier supply chain structure
codes.description: Off-site construction supply chains span factory and site environments, involve numerous tiers (manufacturer, transporter, subcontractor, contractor, developer) and are inherently harder to manage than single-site conventional construction.

codes.label: Mistrust and adversarial contractor-supplier relationships
codes.description: General contractors and subcontractors/manufacturers often have conflicting goals, mistrustful relationships, and risk-transfer tendencies that undermine collaboration in off-site supply chains.

codes.label: Bargaining power asymmetry between contractors and suppliers/developers
codes.description: Contractors typically hold more bargaining power than fabricators, while developers hold dominant power over general contractors, shaping how contractual risk and pricing terms are set.

codes.label: Independent, self-interested decision-making preventing natural JIT
codes.description: Because factories, contractors and developers are independent for-profit entities, just-in-time delivery and supply chain optimisation cannot emerge naturally without financial incentives or coordination mechanisms.

codes.label: Manufacturer serving multiple concurrent clients
codes.description: Off-site manufacturers often serve multiple projects simultaneously, causing resource-planning conflicts that propagate delay risk into a given project's supply chain, a factor not addressed in bilateral contracts.

categories.label: Schedule Deviation, Waste and Compensation Mechanisms
categories.memo: Addresses how deviations between planned and actual delivery/assembly dates generate waste (inventory, overtime, rework) and the contractual/compensation mechanisms proposed to allocate or dynamically price this risk.

codes.label: Waste from non-optimal delivery timing
codes.description: Early or late delivery relative to assembly schedule generates either contractor inventory/storage/double-handling costs or factory overtime/rework costs.

codes.label: Static/fixed compensation and pricing schemes
codes.description: Conventional contracts use static reimbursement or uniform 'blanket agreement' pricing that does not reflect the real-time cost of schedule changes, placing disproportionate responsibility on suppliers/factories.

codes.label: Dynamic, quantitative compensation mechanisms
codes.description: Proposed alternatives use real-time surcharges, incentives, or rebates tied to actual cost of delivery date changes to balance interests between contractor and factory/supplier more directly than fixed terms.

sub_codes.label: Surcharge/incentive-based coordination (inverse Kanban / information platform)
sub_codes.description: An information-sharing platform enabling dynamic release of surcharge/incentive data supports many-to-many contractor-factory coordination while individual transactions remain governed by bilateral contracts.

sub_codes.label: Supplier rebate for delivery-schedule adherence
sub_codes.description: A rebate granted when a contractor accepts shipment per its originally chosen schedule, functioning as a pain-gain sharing mechanism that rewards schedule reliability without centralized control.

codes.label: Contracts as binding fallback despite coordination mechanisms
codes.description: Even where dynamic or collaborative coordination models are proposed, the underlying contract remains the default enforceable mechanism if parties cannot reach a mutually beneficial agreement.

codes.label: Rigid schedule adherence forced by standard contract terms
codes.description: Standard contractual arrangements push both contractors and manufacturers to rigidly follow fixed schedules rather than coordinate on disruptions, turning a pull-based system into a forced push system.

codes.label: Responsibility allocation for implementing JIT production
codes.description: Debate over whether contractors or suppliers/factories should bear primary responsibility for achieving just-in-time delivery performance, with literature favouring greater contractor responsibility.

categories.label: Transport, Logistics Planning and Just-in-Time Delivery
categories.memo: Covers physical transportation and logistics planning of modules/components, the trade-off between transport cost and punctuality, and contractual penalty structures analogous to delay damages.

codes.label: Intuition-based vs optimized transport planning
codes.description: Real-world transport planning of prefabricated modules is often intuitively decided by contractors rather than optimized, leading to unnecessary early/late delivery costs.

codes.label: Trade-off between transportation cost and delivery punctuality
codes.description: Strict JIT adherence requires more frequent, costly deliveries, while minimizing transport cost risks early/late delivery penalties; project planners must balance this trade-off.

codes.label: Penalty costs for early/late delivery as contractual analogue
codes.description: Unit penalty costs for early or late delivery function similarly to contractual delay damages, shaping vehicle routing and delivery timing decisions and informing how penalty clauses could be structured.

codes.label: Cross-border/off-shore transportation and customs risk
codes.description: Transportation of modules across borders or overseas introduces marine, regulatory and customs uncertainties that disrupt contractually planned assembly/delivery schedules and increase logistics costs.

codes.label: Limited on-site storage forcing third-party warehousing
codes.description: Constrained site inventory capacity compels contractors to lease external warehousing or use logistics providers' storage, increasing the cost impact of delivery/assembly mismatches.

codes.label: Contractor risk-averse early-delivery behaviour
codes.description: Contractors often order or accept early delivery of modules/materials to hedge against on-site scheduling uncertainty and late-delivery risk, shifting inventory cost burden to suppliers and generating waste despite JIT goals.

categories.label: Contractual Delivery Deadlines and Module Assembly Scheduling
categories.memo: Focuses on how contract documents formally define delivery deadlines that constrain module fabrication/assembly schedules and how this constrains project planning models.

codes.label: Contract-derived on-site demand deadlines constraining schedules
codes.description: Construction contract documents specify expected delivery times that function as hard constraints on module assembly finish times, requiring buffer time before contractual deadlines.

codes.label: Design freeze and reduced scope for contract variations
codes.description: Once design is frozen for prefabrication, the ability to issue contract variations is reduced, changing how the standard variation/change process operates for MMC compared to conventional construction.

codes.label: Variation orders disrupting supplier delivery cycles
codes.description: Client-initiated variation orders disrupt prefabrication suppliers' preparation, resourcing, quality control and coordination cycles, jeopardizing logistics, scheduling and installation efficiency.

categories.label: Contractual Structures for Third-Party Logistics and Subcontractor Coordination
categories.memo: Addresses how logistics services (e.g., construction logistics modules, TPL providers) and subcontractor obligations are structured, mandated, and coordinated through contracts on projects.

codes.label: Mandatory contractual stipulation of logistics service use
codes.description: Use of construction logistics service modules by subcontractors is often mandated directly in their contracts with the main contractor, reducing voluntary buy-in and delaying value co-creation.

codes.label: Main contractor's dual role as customer and de facto promoter
codes.description: The main contractor simultaneously acts as customer of third-party logistics services and as the party responsible for convincing subcontractors to adopt mandated logistics modules, blending contractual roles.

codes.label: Lack of cross-project continuity in logistics contracting
codes.description: Procurement of new logistics modules for each project resets co-creation and learning processes, reflecting a lack of continuity in contractual/service arrangements across projects.

codes.label: Uncertain risk allocation for resource-related disruptions
codes.description: The unpredictable nature of construction projects makes contracts unclear about who bears responsibility for resource demand fluctuations and related risks.

categories.label: Delivery Method, Procurement Type and Early Supply Chain Integration
categories.memo: Covers how project delivery/procurement method (IPD, Design-Build, traditional DBB) shapes supply chain structure, collaboration potential, and early involvement of suppliers/manufacturers, and how these differ from operational-level compensation mechanisms.

codes.label: Procurement method as determinant of supply chain structure
codes.description: The type of contract procurement or project delivery system used significantly influences and defines the relationships and collaborative potential within the construction supply chain.

codes.label: Integrated/collaborative delivery outperforming traditional DBB for innovative projects
codes.description: Design-Build and other integrated delivery methods show better cost and modification outcomes than traditional Design-Bid-Build for innovative, MMC-related projects, though traditional modes are less suited to innovation.

codes.label: Early supplier/manufacturer/vendor involvement in design
codes.description: Suppliers and manufacturers seek or benefit from early involvement in design phases—sometimes unpaid—to influence design decisions, ensure producibility, and reduce coordination risk between design and production.

codes.label: Integrated Project Delivery for off-site coordination
codes.description: IPD is identified as a relational multiparty contract model suited to off-site prefabrication coordination and strategic supply chain alignment, though it operates at a project/strategic level rather than resolving operational delivery-date issues, and is not a strict prerequisite for prefabrication success.

codes.label: Simplified contractual interfaces via integrated supplier-builder models
codes.description: When a supplier also provides building services, the traditional multi-party supply chain collapses into fewer contractual tiers, simplifying relationships and reducing interfaces.

categories.label: Risk Allocation, Incentives and Subsidy Mechanisms Across the Supply Chain
categories.memo: Covers government and inter-firm incentive/subsidy structures, revenue-sharing and transfer-payment contracts, and broader risk allocation between developers, contractors, manufacturers and suppliers relevant to prefabrication supply chains.

codes.label: Revenue-sharing and transfer-payment contracts between developer and contractor
codes.description: Contractual mechanisms transferring government subsidies via revenue-sharing, combined with transfer payments, are proposed to fairly allocate risk and cost between developers and general contractors and incentivize higher prefabrication/assembly rates.

codes.label: Government subsidy design for MC/PC adoption
codes.description: Government financial subsidies, modeled as a Stackelberg leader-follower relationship with contractors, are more effective than technical guidelines or mandates in driving MMC adoption, though optimal design must account for uncertainty and diminishing returns.

codes.label: Mandatory assembly rate benchmarks as market barriers
codes.description: Government-mandated minimum assembly/prefabrication rates, if set too high, discourage contractor and developer adoption of prefabrication due to increased cost burden, indicating a risk in regulatory/contractual benchmark-setting.

codes.label: Onerous subcontract terms and duplicate sourcing as risk mitigation
codes.description: Large builders impose rigid delivery-regardless-of-circumstances subcontract terms on prefabrication suppliers, or deliberately engage multiple competing suppliers for the same scope, as contractual strategies to mitigate late/failed delivery risk.

codes.label: Financial security instruments in prefabrication contracts
codes.description: Builders use bank guarantees, insurance certificates, and third-party quantity surveyor-approved payment claims to manage cash flow and risk in prefabrication supplier contracts.

codes.label: Vendor partnership agreements as quasi-contractual coordination
codes.description: Legally nonbinding vendor partnership agreements formally allocate responsibilities across communication, materials, delivery, payment, technology and training to support prefabrication supply chain coordination.

codes.label: Transaction costs and reputational risk from design changes
codes.description: Design changes generate significant hidden transaction costs for developers and damage reputation/willingness of other stakeholders to collaborate on future contracts, an overlooked cost risk in prefabrication procurement.

categories.label: Information Sharing, BIM and Communication Coordination Mechanisms
categories.memo: Addresses tools and practices (BIM, labeling systems, communication channels) used to coordinate offsite/onsite information flow, and how poor or outdated communication practices create contractual/coordination risk.

codes.label: BIM and integrated information technologies for supply chain coordination
codes.description: BIM, RFID and GPS are used as coordination tools linking contractors, vendors and manufacturers, improving information transfer, resource sharing, and construction management efficiency.

codes.label: Labeling, packaging and standardization systems for logistical coordination
codes.description: Clear labeling/packaging systems and modularization/standardization of components reduce coordination risk and interfacing effort between offsite fabrication and onsite installation.

codes.label: Outdated communication channels as root cause of coordination failure
codes.description: Reliance on informal, outdated communication methods (email, messaging apps, hard copies) between designer, contractor and manufacturer is identified as a root cause of costly design-change and delivery problems in prefabrication supply chains.

codes.label: Risk network centrality of key supply chain actors
codes.description: Main contractor, manufacturer, and client occupy central roles in propagating and absorbing supply chain risk, indicating where contractual risk allocation and planning responsibility should be focused.

categories.label: Labor Relations and Workforce Coordination in Prefabrication Supply Chains
categories.memo: Covers how labor union relationships and agreements interact with prefabrication adoption and supply chain coordination, distinct from general risk taxonomy in T1.

codes.label: Union relations as enabler or barrier to prefabrication adoption
codes.description: Labor union agreements and resistance to prefabrication/outsourcing, driven by fears of reduced work hours, can significantly constrain or, if negotiated favourably, enable prefabrication implementation.

codes.label: Strategies to mitigate union resistance
codes.description: Approaches such as labor portability agreements, certification programs, and recategorizing prefabricated assemblies as standard catalog products are proposed to circumvent union constraints on outsourced prefabrication.
